title: Kafka: when to use it
seriesDescription: A Kafka deep dive for system design interviews: why Kafka exists, terminology, messages and keys, offsets and replication, when to use it, scalability, hot partitions, fault tolerance, retries, performance and retention.
description: The triggers for putting a queue in the design and for treating Kafka as a stream.
source: Study notes: Kafka deep dive for system design interviews

questions.prompt: Select all situations where adding a message queue is a good idea.

options.text: Work can be asynchronous, so the slow part is done later.
options.why: Yes: like transcoding after upload.

options.text: Messages must be processed in the order they came.
options.why: Yes: ordered per partition.

options.text: Producer and consumer should scale independently.
options.why: Yes: decoupling; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: The result must be returned to the caller in the same millisecond.
options.why: No: a queue adds latency.

questions.explanation: Name the trigger out loud in the interview.

questions.prompt: After a video upload, the standard-definition version is available at once and transcoding happens later. Which trigger is this?

options.text: Asynchronous work: the slow part is handled later through a Kafka topic.
options.why: Right: do the slow part when the system has time.

options.text: Strict ordering of all videos globally for most everyday workloads.
options.why: Not the point here; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Real-time stream aggregation of clicks.
options.why: A different use; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Storing the video inside Kafka for long-term archive.
options.why: Do not store big blobs in Kafka.

questions.explanation: The Kafka message carries the link, not the video.

questions.prompt: Ticketmaster's virtual waiting queue lets users into the booking page in arrival order. Which trigger does this show?

options.text: Order must be kept.
options.why: Right: a queue keeps arrival order.

options.text: Real-time analytics over many consumer groups.
options.why: That is the stream case.

options.text: Caching hot product pages.
options.why: Not related; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Encrypting payments.
options.why: Not related; it does not answer the question asked.

questions.explanation: Kafka preserves order within a partition.

questions.prompt: Which problem is a natural fit for using Kafka as a stream?

options.text: An ad click aggregator that aggregates clicks continuously in real time.
options.why: Right: a continuous flow.

options.text: A one-off nightly report run by one analyst for most everyday workloads.
options.why: Not a continuous flow.

options.text: A static website with no events.
options.why: No events to stream; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: A single file upload with no follow-up processing in a typical production setup.
options.why: Nothing to stream; it does not answer the question asked.

questions.explanation: Real-time flow, or many readers of one log? Think stream.

questions.prompt: Several different services need the same comments, each with its own progress. What makes this work?

options.text: Each consumer group keeps its own offsets over the retained log.
options.why: Right: pub/sub style fan-out.

options.text: All services must share one consumer group as a general rule of thumb.
options.why: They would split the messages instead.

options.text: Each service needs its own Kafka cluster.
options.why: One log can serve many groups.

options.text: Messages are copied by hand into separate topics under normal operating conditions.
options.why: Not needed; it does not answer the question asked.

questions.explanation: FB Live Comments uses Kafka as pub/sub for many consumers.
